descripcion_es: Possessive adjectives and pronouns; the possessive 's (Saxon genitive) and the structure with of.
resumen: Possessive adjectives (my, your, his, her…) go before the noun and agree with the owner, not with the thing owned. To say “of” with people you normally use 's (Ana's car), and with things of (the end of the film).

explicacion.texto: His and her depend on the owner: Juan and his mother, Marta and her father. In Spanish “su” is used for everything; in English you have to choose. The adjective goes with a noun (This is my bag) and the pronoun replaces it (This bag is mine).

items: Possessive 's: owner + 's + thing: my brother's car.
Plural ending in -s: apostrophe only: my parents' house. Irregular plural: the children's toys.
With things, of is preferred: the door of the kitchen, the name of the street.
Its (belonging to a thing) has no apostrophe; it's means it is.

ejemplos.traduccion: Este es el dormitorio de mi hermana.

ejemplos.frase: The dog is eating its dinner.
ejemplos.traduccion: El perro se está comiendo su cena.

ejemplos.frase: I don't remember the title of the song.
ejemplos.traduccion: No recuerdo el título de la canción.

errores_hispanohablantes.nota: The possessive agrees with the owner (Maria = she = her).
With no noun after it you use the pronoun.
The possessive its has no apostrophe.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the right possessive adjective.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule in the table that the possessive agrees with the owner, not with the thing owned. The clue is the subject, Lucía, who is a woman, that is, she, whose possessive adjective is her. It does not matter that grandparents is plural: the possessive does not change according to the thing owned. That is why Lucía's grandparents (Spanish “sus abuelos”) is her grandparents.

errores_previstos.explicacion: His is the possessive for a male owner; Lucía is a woman, so it is her.
Calque of Spanish plural “sus” because abuelos is plural: in English the possessive depends on the owner (Lucía, she), not on the thing owned.
Hers is the pronoun that stands alone; before a noun you use the adjective her.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the right possessive adjective.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule that his and her depend on the owner. The clue is Carlos, a man, that is, he, whose possessive is his. The fact that keys is plural makes no difference: in English possessives do not change for a plural thing owned. That is why Carlos's keys (Spanish “sus llaves”) is his keys.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Her refers to a female owner; Carlos is male: his.
The plural of keys does not affect the possessive, which agrees with Carlos (he): his.
He is the subject pronoun; to show possession you need the adjective his.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the right possessive adjective.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the table of possessive adjectives: the possessive for the subject we is our. The clue is the subject of the sentence, we, which is also the owner of the flat. Our does not change even though the owner is plural, nor according to the gender of the thing owned; in Spanish you would say “nuestro” or “nuestra”, but in English it is always our.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Ours is the pronoun that stands alone (The flat is ours); before a noun you use our.
Us is the object pronoun (They called us); for possession you use our.
Their goes with they; the owner here is we: our.

ejercicios.frase: That isn't my coat. ___ is black.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the difference the card explains between adjective and pronoun: the adjective goes with a noun (my coat) and the pronoun replaces it (mine). The clue is that after the gap there is no noun, but the verb is straight away: you need a word that stands on its own for “my coat”. That is why it is Mine, with a capital letter because it starts the sentence, and with no article before it, unlike Spanish “el mío”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Ese no es mi abrigo. El mío es negro.

errores_previstos.explicacion: My needs a noun after it (My coat is black); on its own you need the pronoun mine.
Calque of Spanish “el mío”: in English the possessive pronoun never takes an article.
Me is the object pronoun; for Spanish “el mío” you use mine.

ejercicios.frase: Those are my parents' bikes. They're ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the column of possessive pronouns in the table: the pronoun for they is theirs. The clue is the owner, my parents, that is, they, and the fact that the gap is at the end, with no noun after it. That is why “they belong to them” is They're theirs. Note that theirs, like hers or ours, has no apostrophe.
ejercicios.traduccion: Esas son las bicis de mis padres. Son suyas.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Their is the adjective and needs a noun after it (their bikes); on its own it is theirs.
Possessive pronouns have no apostrophe: theirs.
Them is the object pronoun; to show they belong to them you need the possessive theirs.

ejercicios.frase: The cat is playing with ___ ball.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the note on the card that its, the possessive of it, has no apostrophe, while it's means it is. The clue is the owner, the cat, an animal normally referred to as it, and the noun ball after the gap, which calls for a possessive adjective. That is why it is its ball. With a pet whose sex you know, his or her is sometimes used, but the neutral and expected form here is its.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Possessive of it: its, with no apostrophe.
ejercicios.traduccion: El gato está jugando con su pelota.

por_opcion.it's: Incorrect: it's is the contraction of it is (or it has); “the cat is playing with it is ball” makes no sense.
por_opcion.its: Correct: possessive of it, with no apostrophe, before the noun ball.
por_opcion.his: Incorrect in the neutral sentence: his is for a male owner. It would only be used if the speaker treats the cat as “he” because it is their pet.

ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the difference between adjective and pronoun on the card: the adjective goes with a noun and the pronoun replaces it. The clue is that the noun phone appears after the gap, so you need the adjective your. If the sentence were “Is this phone ___?”, then yours would be correct.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Before a noun you use the adjective your.

por_opcion.yours: Incorrect here: yours stands alone, with no noun (Is this yours?). With phone after it you need your.
por_opcion.your: Correct: possessive adjective before the noun phone.
por_opcion.you: Incorrect: you is a personal pronoun and does not show possession.

ejercicios.frase: The ___ room is on the left.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule of the possessive 's with irregular plurals: when the plural does not end in -s, like children, you add 's just as in the singular. The clue is that children is already plural and does not end in -s, so the apostrophe goes before the s: children's room. Only plurals ending in -s (parents) take the apostrophe after it.
ejercicios.traduccion: La habitación de los niños está a la izquierda.

por_opcion.children's: Correct: irregular plural with no final -s, so you add 's.
por_opcion.childrens': Incorrect: “childrens” does not exist; children is already plural and takes 's.
por_opcion.childs': Incorrect: “childs” is not the plural of child; besides, the apostrophe after the s is only used with regular plurals in -s.

ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule of the possessive 's: owner + 's + thing. The clue is that the owner is a person, my grandmother, and the card says that with people you normally use 's instead of of. To transform it, the owner moves to the front with 's and the article the disappears, because my grandmother's now does its job: my grandmother's house.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The owner is a person: possessive 's.

errores_previstos.explicacion: When you use the possessive 's, the article the before the thing owned disappears.
The apostrophe is missing: without it, grandmothers looks like a plural.
The 's that marks possession is missing: my grandmother's house.

ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the difference between the adjective her, which goes with a noun, and the pronoun hers, which replaces it. The clue is the instruction to use a possessive pronoun: the noun bag has to disappear from after the possessive. That is why her bag becomes hers, either in This bag is hers or in This is hers. Hers has no apostrophe.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Her bag is replaced by hers.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Her is an adjective or an object pronoun; to say it belongs to her at the end of the sentence you need hers.
Possessive pronouns have no apostrophe: hers.
Calque of Spanish “el suyo”: the English possessive pronoun takes no article.

ejercicios.frase: Ana is talking to his mother.
respuestas: Ana is talking to her mother.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the key rule on the card: his and her depend on the owner. Ana is a woman, so her possessive is her: her mother. The mistake is typical of Spanish speakers, who, since “su” is used for everything, choose his at random or link it to the thing owned. Always ask yourself whose mother it is: Ana's, a woman's, so her.
ejercicios.traduccion: Ana está hablando con su madre.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Ana is talking to his mother.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: his would mean the mother belongs to a man; Ana is a woman, so her.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Ana is talking to hers mother.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Hers stands alone; before the noun you use the adjective her.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Ana is talking to the her mother.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The possessive already does the job of the article: you do not use both.

ejercicios.frase: This is the car of Peter.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule on the card that with people you normally use the possessive 's: owner + 's + thing. The clue is that the owner is Peter, a person. “The car of Peter” is a calque of Spanish “el coche de Peter”: it is understood, but it is not natural. When you change it to Peter's car, the article the disappears.
ejercicios.traduccion: Este es el coche de Peter.

errores_previstos.respuesta: This is the car of Peter.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: with people you use 's, Peter's car.
With the possessive 's you do not put the before the owner.
The apostrophe is missing: Peter's.

ejercicios.frase: My parent's house is very old.
respuestas: My parents' house is very old.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule on the card that plurals ending in -s only add the apostrophe: my parents' house. The clue is the meaning: the house belongs to both parents, so the owner is plural, parents, and it already ends in -s. “My parent's house” would be the house of only one parent, which makes no sense in this context.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Parents is a plural in -s: the apostrophe goes after it.
ejercicios.traduccion: La casa de mis padres es muy antigua.

errores_previstos.respuesta: My parent's house is very old.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: parent's refers to only one parent; with the plural parents the apostrophe goes after the s.

errores_previstos.respuesta: My parents's house is very old.
errores_previstos.explicacion: With plurals in -s you do not add another s: only the apostrophe, parents'.

errores_previstos.respuesta: My parents house is very old.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The apostrophe that marks possession is missing: parents'.

ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule of the possessive 's: owner + 's + thing. The clue is the word brother's, which already has the 's and so must go immediately before the thing owned, computer, with my in front of it. The sentence follows the order subject + verb + complement: This is my brother's computer. With the verb first you make the question, which is also accepted.
ejercicios.traduccion: Este es el ordenador de mi hermano.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Calque of the Spanish order (“el ordenador de mi hermano”): with the possessive 's the owner goes before the thing.
My goes with brother and comes before it: my brother's computer.
The verb is goes after the subject this, not at the end.

descripcion_larga_es: Possessives show who something belongs to: adjectives such as my, your, his or her before the noun, and the possessive 's to say “of” with people (Ana's car). They are essential from day one. Spanish speakers find it hard that his and her depend on the owner and not on the thing owned, because in Spanish “su” is used for everything, and they also find it hard to place the apostrophe correctly.

contexto.que_es: These are the forms that express possession or belonging: possessive adjectives (my, your, his, her, its, our, their), which go before the noun; possessive pronouns (mine, yours, hers…), which replace it; and the possessive 's, owner + 's + thing (my brother's car), the usual alternative to the construction with of.
contexto.por_que_importa: They are used in almost any conversation: family, objects, work. Mixing up his and her changes the meaning of the sentence (whose mother it is) and is one of the most noticeable mistakes Spanish speakers make. The possessive 's is the natural way to say “of” with people; “the car of Peter” is understood, but it clearly sounds foreign.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: When we talk about what belongs to someone or about relationships (my sister, her boss, Peter's car). The signal is the owner: if it is a man, his; if it is a woman, her; if it is a thing or an animal, its. Where Spanish would say “el coche de Pedro”, English prefers Peter's car; with things of is kept (the end of the film).
